about.title: About
about.intro: I'm a senior backend developer and technical lead, working mostly with C# and .NET. I design and modernize enterprise systems, and I lead a team of five developers while staying hands-on in architecture and code.

journey.title: How I got here
journey.text: I started as a full-stack developer maintaining legacy enterprise applications. Over the years I moved into backend architecture for a new platform and, later, into technical leadership. Working with both legacy and modern code shaped how I decide: I weigh business continuity, scalability and maintainability together.

craft.title: Development and leadership
craft.text: I favor Clean Architecture and SOLID because they keep systems easy to change, and I pick tools for the problem at hand. As a technical lead, I review code, mentor developers and help define the engineering standards the team works by.

ai.title: Exploring AI

metadata.title: Football Stat Analytics | Bruno Lucildo
metadata.description: An academic project that analyzes football athlete performance with AI, retrieval and layered answer checks: architecture, decisions and current state.

football.overview: Football Stat Analytics is a command-line application that analyzes football athlete performance with AI. It indexes scouting reports, answers questions grounded in those reports and offers an interactive chat with analyst personas. It is an academic project.
football.challenge: Language models readily produce statements that sound right but have no support: invented numbers, actions the data never mentioned and flattering adjectives. In sports analysis that is worse than no answer. The challenge was to keep every answer tied to the evidence the user supplies or to the reports that were indexed.
football.solution: Answers pass through layers of checking. Deterministic rules enforce the output format and reject unsupported numbers and wording. A semantic verifier, a second model that must quote the evidence, judges each statement. A failed answer gets one automatic correction attempt, and answers based on reports end with a grounding report showing what could be traced back to the retrieved excerpts.
football.architecture: The application is written in TypeScript on Node.js, using native type stripping and the built-in SQLite module. Ingestion extracts text from PDF reports, translates it, splits it into chunks, generates embeddings with the OpenAI API and stores them in SQLite. Retrieval ranks chunks by a hybrid score that combines embedding similarity and keyword overlap, and sends the five best to the answer prompt. The chat keeps its session history in SQLite and summarizes older messages when the context grows. The code separates AI behavior (personas, policies, validation and verification) from storage and retrieval, and 109 automated tests cover it with stubbed model calls, so they run without an API key.

decisions.title: Rules in code, not only in prompts.
decisions.text: Prompt instructions alone cannot guarantee that the model follows a policy, so the most important rules are checked by code.

decisions.title: A judge that is not trusted blindly.
decisions.text: The verifier must quote the evidence, and a quote that is not in the evidence is rejected. If the verifier itself fails, the chat keeps working and shows a warning.

decisions.title: Optional consensus, off by default.
decisions.text: Answering with the median of three samples costs three times the generation and did not make the scores reliably stable, so it is available but disabled.

decisions.title: Simple local storage.
decisions.text: Conversation history and embeddings live in SQLite files, which keeps the project easy to run and inspect.

football.state: In development. The project describes itself as experimental: answers are not checked against official statistics, PDF ingestion does not run OCR, and the checks are safeguards that do not replace human review. A known limitation is retrieval: the index has no athlete metadata to filter on, so a question about one athlete can retrieve excerpts about others.

metadata.title: Reelix | Bruno Lucildo
metadata.description: A personal movie and series tracking app with privacy-first sharing and spoiler control: architecture, technical decisions and current state.

reelix.overview: Reelix is an app to discover and track movies and series, record what you have watched and share authorized activity with friends. The repository holds a React Native mobile app and an ASP.NET Core API. It is a personal project.
reelix.challenge: A viewing diary is personal data. Sharing it with friends only works if each person controls what is shared, and comments and ratings must not spoil a plot for someone who has not watched yet. The challenge was to build social features on top of that, with privacy and spoiler control as rules of the product rather than afterthoughts.
reelix.solution: Sharing is opt-in and split into separate consents for history, ratings and favorites. Comments are private by default, can be flagged as spoilers and stay hidden until the reader chooses to reveal them. Progress tracking, lists, achievements and a monthly ranking among friends are built on the same rules.
reelix.architecture: The API is a modular monolith in ASP.NET Core (.NET 10), organized in Domain, Application, Infrastructure and Api projects so that business rules do not depend on frameworks or the database. Data lives in PostgreSQL through Entity Framework Core. Supabase Auth handles sign-in, and the API validates its tokens and maps them to the internal account. Movie and series metadata comes from TMDB, behind an adapter, with provider credentials kept on the server. The mobile app uses React Native with Expo, strict TypeScript, Expo Router and TanStack Query. A GitHub Actions workflow runs the backend tests, the mobile lint and type checks, dependency audits and secret scanning.

decisions.title: A modular monolith before microservices.
decisions.text: The design stays simple until real usage justifies more infrastructure.

decisions.title: One identity system.
decisions.text: Supabase Auth is the only provider, and a second system such as ASP.NET Identity was deliberately not added.

decisions.title: Providers behind an adapter.
decisions.text: The catalog integration can be replaced without touching business rules, and provider keys never reach the app.

decisions.title: AI kept off until decided.
decisions.text: An automatic spoiler classifier exists on the server but is disabled by default while cost and data policy are decided; manual spoiler flagging works without it.

reelix.state: In development. The code covers accounts, onboarding, discovery, tracking, lists, ratings and comments, friends, notifications and achievements, but the repository itself states that this describes the implementation and does not confirm a production deployment. Remote push notifications are disabled, the Android widget is not implemented and the mobile app has no automated tests yet.

log.title: Research log
log.intro: The experiments in the order they appear in the lab, with what each one taught me. There are no dates: this is a path, not a calendar.

ragGrounding.name: Grounded answers over reports (RAG)
ragGrounding.summary: Answering questions about scouting reports using only retrieved excerpts, and showing how much of each answer can be traced back to them.
ragGrounding.objective: Answer questions about scouting reports using only what the reports say, and make it visible how much of each answer is actually supported.
ragGrounding.problem: A model asked about reports it has not read invents plausible details: numbers, sources and actions. Citing a source does not prove that the source says it.
ragGrounding.approach: Report PDFs are turned into text, translated from Spanish to Brazilian Portuguese, split into chunks and stored with embeddings in SQLite. A question retrieves the five most relevant chunks, ranked by a hybrid score that combines embedding similarity with keyword overlap and discards weak matches. The prompt requires a source after each statement and runs at temperature 0. Every answer then ends with a grounding report: a lexical check of how many statements, numbers and cited sources appear in the retrieved text, followed by a semantic check made by a second model call.
ragGrounding.results: In the evaluation, a question supported by the reports was answered with the semantic check passing, and questions the reports could not answer (a past tournament winner, a player's salary) were declined as expected. One question written afterwards failed: retrieval ranked the right report first but filled the other four slots with excerpts about other athletes, and the model declined. Only a handful of RAG questions were tested, so this shows behavior, not a failure rate.
ragGrounding.limitations: The index has no athlete metadata to filter on, so a question about one athlete can retrieve excerpts about others. PDF extraction does not use OCR, so scanned reports may yield no text. The relevance score ranks excerpts; it does not measure confidence or truth. The lexical check is not semantic, and answers are not compared with official statistics.
ragGrounding.learned: A citation proves nothing by itself: what helped was showing, next to the answer, what could and could not be traced. A retrieval failure looks like a model failure, so the two are worth measuring apart.

outputValidation.name: Validating model output with rules and a judge model
outputValidation.summary: Checking what a language model says with rules in code and a second model that has to quote the evidence.
outputValidation.objective: Keep every statement an analyst persona makes tied to the evidence the user supplied.
outputValidation.problem: Prompt instructions alone do not guarantee that a model follows a policy. In the first live tests it produced flattering adjectives, actions the data never mentioned and scores for attributes without evidence.
outputValidation.approach: Deterministic rules enforce the answer format and reject numbers, adjectives and actions that are not in the user's input. A semantic verifier, a second model, judges each remaining statement and must quote the evidence; a quote that is not in the evidence is rejected, and if the verifier itself fails, the answer is accepted with a warning. A rejected answer gets one automatic correction attempt that lists the violated rules. A live evaluation harness runs the real model on fixed cases and on cases written afterwards, and reports how many answers pass.
outputValidation.results: On the cases that guided the fixes, answers valid on the first attempt went from 0 of 15 to 12 of 15 over four runs, and 14 of 15 after the correction attempt; that last figure is optimistic, because the fixes were made on those same cases. On a second round written afterwards, 43 of 48 answers were valid on the first attempt and 48 of 48 after the correction (22 of 24 and 24 of 24 on those cases alone). An embedded instruction to give every attribute 99 did not change the scores. Calibrating the verifier on 30 statements labelled by the author, over three repetitions it rejected 41 of 45 unsupported statements and accepted 42 of 45 supported ones.
outputValidation.limitations: The rules are lexical, check number words only up to fifty and cannot prove that every sentence is correct. The judge is itself a model: it consistently accepted one false claim of missing data. The labels were set by the author alone, and 30 statements and 15 answers per run are small samples that describe this setup, not a general error rate. The model is not fully deterministic: one score varied by ten points between runs at temperature 0. None of this replaces human review.
outputValidation.learned: Measure with cases written after the fixes, or the numbers flatter the work. A verifier should not be trusted blindly: requiring a quote made it checkable. The check costs an extra request per answer, the price of fewer unsupported statements.

scoreConsistency.name: Median of three samples for stable scores
scoreConsistency.metaTitle: Median of three for stable scores
scoreConsistency.summary: Testing whether answering with the median of three samples makes a model's scores stable.
scoreConsistency.objective: Find out whether any mode makes the scores for the same input reliable from one run to the next.
scoreConsistency.problem: The same input can produce different scores from the same model, even at temperature 0, which undermines a score that people might act on.
scoreConsistency.approach: Each of six athlete cases was answered eight times per mode (temperature 0 with and without a seed, and the median of three samples at two temperatures), and the score vectors were compared. Only the deterministic validation was applied. The experiment ran twice, with 48 answers per mode and run.
scoreConsistency.results: No mode made the scores reliably stable: the case that varied changed between runs, and the same mode went from a largest spread of 1 point to 8 between two executions. The seed did not help consistently. The median vote was the only mode in which every answer was valid, because it discards invalid samples.
scoreConsistency.limitations: Six cases and two runs are a small sample. The variation comes from the model, so tuning these settings cannot remove it. The median costs three times the generation. Computing the scores in code from the cited indicators would remove the variation, but it would turn qualitative judgments into a formula, so it was not done.
scoreConsistency.learned: A negative result is still a result: it settled the decision to keep the consensus available but off by default. Consistency is something to measure, not to assume.

analystPersonas.name: Analyst personas built with prompts
analystPersonas.summary: Designing analyst personas with prompts, conversation history and simple input and output checks.
analystPersonas.objective: Explore how far prompts alone can shape an assistant for football analysis.
analystPersonas.problem: The same model should behave differently when it assesses a player's performance, a transfer proposal or a tactical reading, and each task needs its own rules about what counts as evidence.
analystPersonas.approach: A terminal chatbot in TypeScript sends messages to the OpenAI API and streams the answer. Three personas carry their own instructions: sports analysis, transfer-proposal analysis and tactical analysis. The conversation is stored in SQLite, with utilities to limit or summarize the history, and simple checks screen input and output.
analystPersonas.results: No formal evaluation was done in this experiment: the checks are textual heuristics and the repository has no test suite. The same personas are part of Football Stat Analytics, where validation and measurement were built.
analystPersonas.limitations: The checks do not guarantee that an answer is correct or safe. The repository has no install or run instructions yet, so the experiment cannot be reproduced from it, and it is separate from the future FintaLab product.
analystPersonas.learned: Without tests or measurements there is no way to tell whether a persona follows its instructions, which is the gap the validation and evaluation experiments address.

approachAndModelChoice.name: Choosing an approach and a model
approachAndModelChoice.metaTitle: Choosing an approach and a model
approachAndModelChoice.summary: Comparing rules, machine learning, language models and a hybrid design, then three models, to decide how to automate football performance analysis.
approachAndModelChoice.objective: Decide, before building anything, which kind of technology fits each part of a football performance analysis, and which language model to start with.
approachAndModelChoice.problem: Every option has strengths and costs: fixed rules are predictable but rigid, language models read free text well but can be inconsistent or wrong, and cost and delay differ between models. Choosing by habit or by hype leaves those trade-offs unrecorded.
approachAndModelChoice.approach: I compared four approaches (deterministic rules, machine learning, a language model and a hybrid) across ten criteria, such as flexibility, consistency, ease of validation, operating cost and risk of incorrect analyses. Then I compared three language models (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet and Llama 3 70B) on quality, consistency, latency, cost and fit for the case. Both comparisons use qualitative levels and 1-to-5 scores that I assigned in a planning exercise.
approachAndModelChoice.results: A decision, not a measurement: a hybrid design, with rules for calculations and objective criteria, machine learning where classification is needed and a language model to interpret and write analyses, always behind output validation and human review for critical cases. For the pilot the model chosen was Claude Sonnet, for its balance of quality, consistency and moderate cost. No scores are published here, because they were judgments, not measurements.
approachAndModelChoice.limitations: The levels and scores are qualitative and have no stated measurement method, so they must not be read as a model ranking. The comparison was made at planning time, before the experiments on this page existed: those run on gpt-4o-mini, not on the model chosen for the pilot, and the scores were never checked against them. Cost and latency depend on the provider, the date and the infrastructure.
approachAndModelChoice.learned: Writing the trade-offs down makes the choice open to discussion. The experiment on validating model output is one way of applying the hybrid idea: rules and a verifier around the model, because the model alone does not guarantee consistency.

promptTestFramework.name: A test framework for prompts
promptTestFramework.summary: A method to test a prompt like software: fixed cases, repeated runs, scored criteria, failures traced to causes and a retest after each fix.
promptTestFramework.objective: Define a repeatable way to judge whether a prompt that turns athlete data into scored attributes is accurate, consistent and honest when data is missing.
promptTestFramework.problem: A response that merely looks right is not evidence. The same prompt can invent a statistic, overvalue volume over efficiency or give different answers to the same case, and an edit to the prompt can fix one problem and cause another.
promptTestFramework.approach: The framework defines eight criteria, each scored from 1 to 5: accuracy, adherence to the data, consistency, completeness, justification, hallucination, score coherence and format. It uses ten test cases covering simple, complex, ambiguous, extreme and reliability situations (for example, many shots with low efficiency, missing data, contradictory indicators and a request for information that was never provided), each meant to run three times with the same input. Failures are linked to a hypothesis about the prompt, the prompt is rewritten as explicit, checkable rules, and the same cases run again. The cycle is: test, find failures, analyze causes, fix the prompt, retest and validate.
promptTestFramework.results: No results are published for this experiment. The tables in the original document are an illustrative scenario, written to show how failures would be identified and traced, not a record of measured runs.
promptTestFramework.limitations: It is a method, not a measurement: there is no published evidence about a real prompt. Ten cases with three runs each are a small sample, the 1-to-5 scores are assigned by a person, and a clean retest does not guarantee that new errors will not appear, so the cycle has to be repeated whenever the prompt, the model or the indicators change.
promptTestFramework.learned: Turning vague instructions into rules that can be checked is what makes a fix testable. The framework puts missing data and unanswerable requests among the cases because that is where a model is most tempted to invent something.

loraFineTuning.name: Fine-tuning a small model to classify reviews (LoRA)
loraFineTuning.summary: Fine-tuning a 1.5-billion-parameter model with LoRA to classify short football performance reviews, and what the evaluation does and does not show.
loraFineTuning.objective: Find out whether a LoRA adapter makes a small open model better at labelling a performance review as positive, neutral or negative, and at answering in a format a program can read.
loraFineTuning.problem: Small models often ignore the required answer format or lean toward the wrong label, and classifying reviews by hand does not scale. Fine-tuning is a candidate fix, but only a fair evaluation can say whether it helps.
loraFineTuning.approach: The base model, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, was loaded with 4-bit quantization on a Colab T4 GPU and trained with a LoRA adapter (rank 16, alpha 32, on the attention query and value projections) for three epochs, with a system instruction and a JSON answer holding a single sentiment field. The training set was one file of 75 short reviews, 25 per class. The comparison switches the adapter off and on over the same model, with greedy decoding, and counts correct labels, invalid answers and a confusion matrix.
loraFineTuning.results: On the same 75 reviews used for training, the model without the adapter labelled 55 correctly and the adapted model 63. Invalid answers fell from 13 of 75 to 1 of 75. Negative reviews found rose from 14 of 25 to 22 of 25, and positive reviews from 23 of 25 to 25 of 25, while neutral reviews found fell from 18 of 25 to 16 of 25 and neutral reviews labelled positive grew from 5 of 25 to 9 of 25. Because these reviews were also the training data, the counts show what the adapter learned, not how it would perform on new reviews.
loraFineTuning.limitations: There is no held-out test set. The write-up of the exercise describes a stratified split with one fifth of the data held out, but the notebook I kept evaluates the whole file it trained on, so I treat every count above as measured on training data and as no evidence of generalization. 75 reviews, one run and one seed are a very small sample, with no confidence interval. Label quality depends on how clearly positive, neutral and negative were defined, and ambiguous examples hurt both training and evaluation. One answer from the adapted model was still invalid, and neutral descriptions of facts (a yellow card, having started the match) drifted toward positive. It is not ready for unattended use.
loraFineTuning.learned: A higher count is not evidence until the test data is kept apart from training: here the same file feeds both, so the table cannot say whether the adapter generalizes. Counting format failures separately from labelling errors, and looking at which examples drifted, taught more than the headline number. Next time I would split the data first, freeze the test set and repeat with other seeds.
